Issued at 300 PM EDT Mon Oct 5 2026

Now-Tonight...The current satellite presentation is very similar to 
this time yesterday: clouds reaching the I-4 corridor from the west 
coast of FL as low-level cumulus forms across the remainder of the 
area. All ECFL locations are dry for now, but that looks to change 
later this afternoon and evening as storm chances grow. Southerly 
surface flow will likely delay the westward push of the east coast 
breeze until mid afternoon. Already, satellite is showing some 
congested cumulus along the forming breeze, and KMLB/KVRB/KSUA winds 
have veered east-southeasterly. 

Various CAMs suggest isolated to scattered storm coverage along the 
breeze after 1-2 PM along the I-95 corridor. Later, attention turns 
toward interior locations as the west and east coast breezes move 
inland, eventually colliding near I-4. With this additional forcing, 
plus a weak front settling over the area this evening, coverage of 
showers and storms is likely to increase after 5-6 PM. Light but 
persistent westerly steering flow above 700mb suggests rain and 
storms should push back east toward the Atlantic coast well beyond 8-
9 PM. The risk for lightning and gusty winds is forecast to 
gradually diminish after sunset, but locally heavy rain will remain 
possible. Higher rain rates will lead to a quick 1-3" in spots with 
some indication of locally higher amounts reaching 4"+, especially 
from the Orlando metro to Cape Canaveral/Melbourne. Much of the area 
is in a Marginal Risk (level 1 of 4) for Excessive Rainfall today, 
highlighting the potential for minor flooding. Standing water on 
roads and in low-lying/urban areas may occur quickly, so take this 
into account during evening commute times. Avoid flooded roadways!

Drier conditions are forecast overnight but an isolated shower or 
two cannot be completely discounted along the I-4 corridor and 
immediate coastline. Temperatures settle into the 70s for most with 
the coolest spots north of I-4.

Tuesday-Wednesday...A frontal boundary is forecast to stall over top 
of or just north of the area mid week, helping to prolong an above-
average rainfall pattern. Weak upper level ridging with a longwave 
trough (well north) over the Great Lakes will sustain west-
southwesterly flow aloft. Saturated sounding profiles suggest we 
will stick with a lot of cloud cover for much of this period, with 
occasional hints of clearing. High moisture content combined with a 
stalled front leads to the widely advertised 60-85% rain chances 
each day. Lightning chances may peak earlier in the afternoon and 
across across southern locations before scattered/numerous showers 
and associated clouds limit overall instability. Generally speaking, 
1-2" of rain is anticipated for much of the area from Tuesday 
morning through Wednesday night. Pockets of locally higher amounts 
(2-4") are expected, especially where repeated rounds of rain occur. 
Increasingly saturated soils and runoff will support local instances 
of flooding, especially in poor drainage and urban areas. Based on 
the latest QPF amounts, areas from Orlando/Cape Canaveral northward 
have a 40% or greater chance at receiving at least 2" of rain 
through Thursday morning. 

Depending on how far the stalled front sinks to the south, northerly 
winds look to increase along the Volusia Coast Wednesday (gusts 25-
30+ in the afternoon). This will create hazardous surf conditions 
and elevate the risk for life-threatening rip currents north of Cape 
Canaveral.

Temperatures will reflect the added clouds/rain especially across 
the northern half of the area. Near to above normal temps are 
forecast from Orlando southward on Tuesday with values in the lower 
80s across the north. On Wednesday, much of the area only reaches 
the low to mid 80s, except along the Treasure Coast, which may still 
push the upper 80s.

Thursday-Sunday...Low pressure over the central Gulf is being 
monitored for tropical development later this week. Ridging briefly 
builds over the Midwest, allowing for this area of low pressure to 
lift north toward the central Gulf Coast by the weekend. As the 
system moves farther north, it may be able to pull our stationary 
front with it and gradually reduce rain chances by Saturday or 
Sunday. However, there is plenty of uncertainty in any one given 
solution, and maintaining medium to high rain chances through the 
weekend is warranted for now. Scattered to widespread showers and 
occasional lightning storms will peak in coverage each day but 
showers could linger each night (20-40% chance). The threat for 
locally heavy rain is expected to continue, along with the risk for 
flooding. Breezy conditions are forecast each afternoon north of I-4
